utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, everybody. All the accused are here. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Mitchell. Defence, I only notice the absence of Mr. Haynes. Yes, good morning to you, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, just a few more questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Gavrilovic.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just a few more questions and I'll be through. I just want to ask you a little bit about after you spoke the first time, I think you said you thought it was either in March or April to the investigator for Mr. Beara, was it Mr. Stanic, was that the name?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Yes, Mr. Stanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, after he left, what did you say to Mira Cekic about the subject matter that you discussed with Mr. Stanic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told her that he had asked me if I remembered the 14th of July 1995, and that that was the evening when she invited me, or rather, called me by phone, told me that Ljubisa and Nada will be at their place that evening, and asked me if my husband and I wanted to see them. And I was supposed to remember what we talked about that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And how long after Mr. Stanic left did you --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And how long after you spoke to Mr. Stanic that day did you speak to Mira about this?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very next day I called her because I couldn't find her that evening. I called her the following day. After that that Mr. Stanic came to see me, and asked me if I wanted to give my account of what happened on that day, so during the morning on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And, so, then you told Mira your best recollections about that birth day and everything you remembered, I take it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, there was no need for that; she was there, too. It was in their home; although, she wasn't there the whole time because she was the hostess and she would go to and fro to the kitchen to bring out the food et cetera. Basically, she knew what we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But as you told me before, you said "I told her that he had asked me if I remembered the 14th of July 1995, that that was the evening when she invited me, or rather, that called me by phone, told me that Ljubisa and Nada will be at their place that evening, and asked me if my husband and I wanted to see them. And I was supposed to remember what we had talked about." So you went over all that with her?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, basically, yes. But it wasn't so necessary because we were all together at that place that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But this had been a long time ago, and by talking with Mira, you were able to help her remember it, too, I take it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. She did remember because Toma, her husband, was making jokes about our failed trip on the Orient Express, by saying that there was a newly opened restaurant in our city named the Orient Express and it's decorated in the same way, and he told us to go there and imagine that we were on the trip. So she clearly remembered that joke of his. So she remembered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sure. Okay. And when did you see her in person after that, that phone conversation that you talked about right after you talked to Mr. Stanic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly, maybe two weeks after that or three weeks after that. We are not seeing each other on a daily basis. We just meet occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, as you sit here, you can't really remember whether it was -- you know, when you actually met with her to see her face to face? Can you roughly give me an -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean what was the occasion for the two of us to get together, is that what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. I'm just trying to get an idea of when it was you met with her face to face?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After my conversation with Mr. Stanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About how long?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I would say some two weeks later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where was it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At my place. She dropped by because, as I told you, I'm in the cosmetics business. She had some problems with her face, she came to me to -- for some treatment, and that is when we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I get this picture in my head, and maybe I've seen too many movies, in the beauty parlour, with you working on her, and you are talking to her about everything, right, something like that? Is that right or is that just --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then you discussed the matter with her at that time?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I talked to my clients about various things, and the same applies to you. We talk about our families, about the problems that I'm having with my son who is at the university and is not doing very well. We also mentioned Nada, and we said that we were sorry that everything happened to them in the way that it did, that they were good people, so on so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you did talk about Nada Beara's husband and his problems, and the things that you've been talking about today and yesterday, with Mira?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We mostly talked about Nada and their children; that is to say, the people who remained in our city. We used to go and visit them. So we basically talked about Nada and her personal problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That I don't want to, of course, get into. I'm just interested in the party back in 1995 and the subject matter that Mr. Stanic talked to you about. You've told us you talked to Nada about that, too, at the beauty parlour, I take it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Mira?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We discussed it and we were wondering whether we would have to go to The Hague to talk about it, so that was the essence of it, whether that would be a pleasant or an unpleasant experience for us and that if we must do it, we will do so and to tell what we know and what the truth is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you must know that Mira is here as well; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you have had a chance to talk again with Mira before you both came to The Hague about the topic that Mr. Stanic talked to you about?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there was no reason for that because what I'm telling you now is really the truth and what is she going to tell you will also be the truth, and if we discussed anything that was only the truth about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sure, it's normal for witnesses that got to come to this place to talk about, you know, what they are going to say with each other, especially if it's the same topic. That's normal. I'm just asking you when was it before coming to The Hague. The last time before you came to The Hague, did you talk to Mira in Belgrade about this topic that you discussed with Mr. Stanic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we talked about this -- well, not about the topic itself. We rather talked about how we have to travel, how shall we prepare ourselves. As I say, there was no need because we were at her place. Everything happened at her place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You didn't talk about the party at all with her before you came -- right before you came to Belgrade -- sorry, right before you came to The Hague from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But where did you speak to her about your trip to The Hague, was it your place, her place, over the phone?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked on the phone before the departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What day?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We arrived here on the 24th, so about two days before that. I should say, the 21st or the 22nd, I'm not quite sure. But we just discussed what clothes we should bring, whether it was cold there or warm, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I got a bit ahead of myself, but I want to ask you the same sorts of questions about Nada Beara. So, after Mr. Stanic spoke to you back in what you say is March or April for the first time, did you contact Nada Beara after that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When was the first time after Mr. Stanic talked to you that you had spoken to Nada about this issue, the birthday party?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never discussed the birthday party with Nada. Nada had found out that I was going to The Hague to testify perhaps some five days before our departure. We didn't want to bother her. She had enough stress and enough problem because she would probably be very worried about why we have to go through this unpleasantness of appearing before this court and things like that. So we didn't really want to cause anxiety for her. She actually didn't know that I was summoned as a witness here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So you've never talked to Nada about the birthday party at all?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So your experience hasn't been too bad here, has it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA GAVRILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It hasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much for coming. Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. McCloskey. Is there re-examination Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said -- Mr. Nikolic answered in the negative. So Madam Gavrilovic, as I promised to you yesterday, we have concluded with your testimony. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over to give testimony in this trial, and I also wish you on behalf of everyone a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine there are no documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing from the Prosecution, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That concludes the testimony of Madam Gavrilovic. We had -- we were told before we started the sitting, Mr. Ostojic, that you wished to address the Chamber soon after the conclusion of this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Thank you very much. Two just rather brief housekeeping matters. One is yesterday, when we tendered the Exhibits 2DIC, 210, 211, and 212, these documents were previously identified and entered into evidence under seal. So we would just ask the Court that those documents that bear the number 2DIC, 210, 211, 212 also be placed under seal, because I think the name is reflected for some of the intercept operators. Okay. That would be the first item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The seconds item: We met or I met with the Prosecution last night to discuss scheduling and whatnot, and we'd like to have the Court's understanding on a couple of issues. We do have witnesses here, we are ready to proceed until tomorrow, we are just not sure how long the witnesses will take. We may have a witness. And after I spoke with the Prosecution, we thought we had a deal and an understanding; and when I got back home, I called some of the witnesses. I'm going to have to restructure some of the witness schedule for next week. The Prosecution also made a request of us for one witness later in the week next week to schedule him for the 8th of September, which is the following Monday, because an outside counsel will attempt to be present either via videolink or telephone. We are going to accommodate that request for many different reasons including personal reasons, but we just have to rework the schedule a little bit. So today I'm confident that we can proceed with Mr. Alaica, Mrs. Cekic, and Mr. Milan Kerkez, and that would be it for today, if we get through all three. And tomorrow we are still working on it because I have to meet with my expert, who was scheduled for tomorrow, to see if we should proceed with him. Although I indicated to my learned friends that we were going to proceed with Mr. Subotic tomorrow, Mr. Professor Wagenaar would like to proceed tomorrow. So I have to get back to you specifically on what the order is after these final three witnesses today and tomorrow, so just so that the Court is aware of it and my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll await further information from you. In the meantime, there are a few housekeeping matters and issues that we would like to raise ourselves. One is the following: Mr. Ostojic, way back on the 1st of July, you had filed a motion for witness Osman. Dizdarevic to be heard by video conference link. There was some oral argument on this on the following day, on the 2nd July; then, subsequently, we noticed that on the 17th of July, you filed a fresh 65 ter witness list in which it seemed that Dizdarevic was being withdrawn as a witness. If you confirmed that, can we safely proceed to declare your motion as moot?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We may, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that motion of the 1st of July relating to the testimony of Osman Dizdarevic is being declared moot. Mr. Bourgon and Mrs. Nikolic and Mr. McCloskey, on the 29th of July, there was a motion on behalf of accused Nikolic requesting protective measures and delayed disclosure of the identity of a particular witness with confidential annexes A and B. On the 31st of July, the Prosecution, according to our records, stated that it had no objection to the protective measures sought to wit pseudonym, facial, and voice distortion, and that it had agreed with the Defence that the identity of the witness would be disclosed in the week of 18th August. I personally, then, had stated that once we received a confirmation that the identity of the witness had been disclosed, the protective measures would -- could then be granted. First, therefore, we would like to know from you particularly, Mr. McCloskey, whether the identity of this witness was disclosed to you prior or by the 18th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And there is, then, agreement that we grant the protective measures sought, which are being hereby granted; that is, pseudonym, facial, and voice distortion. The pseudonym details will be communicated to you in due course. Mr. Ostojic, again, and Mr. McCloskey, very recently, and I must say quite belatedly, the Beara Defence team filed another motion seeking the testimony of Seymour Jovanovic to be heard via video conference. There was further detail. There are the reasons why particularly because he is unable to fly to The Hague in the condition he finds himself in. Now, according to the schedule that we had to date, which I understand may be the subject of some changes now, Mr. Ostojic, this gentleman, Seymour Jovanovic, is the third witness who was scheduled to testify next week in the week of 1st September; that is, at least according to the note as you filed in August, on the 15th of August. We haven't heard a response from the Prosecution as yet, and we would therefore, first and foremost, like to know if the Prosecution is in a position to give us their position on this motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, my understanding of this is that this is some kind of medical situation and that we got, of course, in Serbian, and we are in the process of going through this to determine what the medical situation is. I don't have a -- we don't have a firm idea on that yet, but I should very soon. I think we can double check today. Ms. Soljan is not with us this week, but we will try to get at that. Some of the medical terms and things and the Latin has slightly delayed it. I don't know if there's Latin in these ones, but we issue be able to sort that out very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, Mr. Ostojic, can you give us an indication of when he is likely to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If the Court -- and we understand it was perhaps delayed as the Court notices and mentions. We were just made aware of it at the time of our filing. So we didn't appreciate perhaps -- obviously, he is an older gentleman, and he provided us that information. When he did, we submitted it. I think it is in part in English actually, the medical record that we attach. But we've, I think, indicated to the court officer, because I know it takes time to schedule it, that we would call him, I think, on the 9th or 10th or at the convenience of the Court and the Prosecution. He was initially set by our scheduling for next week; but given his condition, I'm sure that we'll accommodate whatever schedule the Court allows to accommodate the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's work on the assumption - it being a medical case - let's work on the assumption that the motion will not be opposed and will be granted, and that's only for argument sake. Start working out with the office the details. Try and schedule his testimony as soon as possible, please, because my understanding --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- is that a minimum of a week's notice is at least required, if not 10 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's why we suggested the 9th or 10th approximately. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, we had an unfortunate incident. We call it "unfortunate" because had you heeded our advisories, we would not have arrived to that stage. Way back on the 31st of July just before we went into recess, following several exchanges between Mr. Ostojic and the Prosecution, we had asked you to identify who the first ten witnesses were going to be after the break; then find out whether in relation to any of these ten witnesses there is still any outstanding dispute between you as to the efficiency or otherwise of the summary, and if there are to sort these out for the time being. We noted positively that the Beara team in the meantime has filed a number of revised 65 ter witness summaries over the recess, and in its 18th August filing added that it will provide additional 65 ter summaries for remaining witness in a short time. We would like to know, especially since you confirmed that there was another meeting yesterday evening, we would like to know whether any further information has been shared, and, in particular, in relation to the next witness Milan Alaica, who we've still got to authorize to be added to the 65 ter witness list.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think, with the next witness, we should be proceeding with no problems. And, I think, with the balance of the witnesses today, it's my understanding that we did provide for Mr. Kerkez and for Ms. Cekic supplemental 65 ter summaries based on our meetings with them in Belgrade a week or two weeks ago, immediately prior to the start of the trial again. But I understand with Mr. Milan Alaica that I think our 65 ter summary was adequate. I think they had enough information yesterday. At our meeting, we did not discuss that specifically, and I don't believe there was an issue raised in connection with that particular witness. We did raise other witnesses. If the Court would like, I can set forth. One witness I think the Prosecution asked for me to give the draft affidavit that we had submitted to him and the changes that were made, I'm looking to provide that to him. I hope to get that to my learned friends by the end of the week, or tomorrow essentially, to provide a copy of that to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We indicate, in particular, that Milan Alaica was amongst those whose witness summaries was considered to be insufficient, together with the following four witnesses that we are pointing out to you for further action if necessary: One is 2DW55, the other one is 2DPW16, then 2DW21, 2DWPW20. These witnesses are already scheduled. Now, whether they will remain scheduled or not is another matter, since Mr. Ostojic is revisiting his list. Then there are these witnesses: 2DW50; Milos Tomovic. Those are two witnesses. Then 2DW77 and Doctor Srdja Trifkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, Mr. McCloskey, it's up to you to state or confirm whether you are happy with the summaries of these individuals or not. With regard to the others, we believe that the summaries are sufficient. Now, in relation -- yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the next witness, we did get an additional summary for; and, as far as we know, we are okay. We've been, of course, continuing discussions with the Beara team, and we still have some outstanding requests for more details. And we still go back and forth, we talk all the time, John and I were just speaking just now. And to get really precise information for you on some of those others, I would need a quick check with Mr. Thayer who is the most knowledgeable on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, one further thing in relation to this next witness, who has strictly speaking not yet been added to the 65 ter witness list, the Prosecution had also objected on the basis that they considered his evidence would be evidence to be commutative to evidence on accused Beara's good character or lack of discriminatory intent and, therefore, not admissible. We have taken stock of this submission which was formalized in a motion earlier on, and we noticed that of the eight witnesses on Beara's good character and/or lack of discriminatory intent whom the Prosecution have challenged, two have been withdrawn and one has already testified. Do you still maintain your position now as to the remaining witnesses, Mr. McCloskey? Do you still maintain your op position, or do you wish to withdraw your opposition to the remaining witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just discuss that with Mr. Thayer, and he is prepared to talk or to inform the Court about those other witnesses you mentioned about where we are on that. So if you could just excuse me for a second, I think we can sort this out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, Mr. McCloskey, can we decree or grant the motion so far as the next witness is concerned, Milan Alaica?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't see any reason why not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So the motion insofar as witness Milan Alaica is being granted. And, Madam Usher, you can start preparing the witness to bring him into the courtroom, please. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hadn't registered your presence in the courtroom before, because the column obstructed the view.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. I can address some of those issues, Mr. President. With respect to the Witness 2DW55, who has as his temporary pseudonym 2DPW16 - they are the same person - we have received an actual proofing note with respect to that individual. And that individual I think will be the subject of some discussion here, and as well as the subject of what Mr. Ostojic referred to previously in terms of rescheduling. That is the witness to whom he was referring scheduling for the week of 8 September. With respect to 2DW21, my belief is that that witness has already testified, if I've got the number right. Milan Vojinovic. I believe, in fact, I think I may have cross-examined him. So, yeah, I think that may be a moot issue. And, again, I may not have gotten the number correct, but 2DWPW20, we've got no record of. I'm not sure if there's a name, if we can said it in open court, that the Trial Chamber has attach to that, that would be helpful, but that number is not popping up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Maybe I could help. I thought we had him as Vasovic Perica, who also testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: He has testified. If it is 2DW20, then he has already come and gone. So, with respect to those summaries, I think we are okay. I've sent an e-mail to my friends, we've had some discussions, we do have some outstanding requests with respect to three of the upcoming witnesses: 2DW5, Mr. Mitrovic; 2DW50; and 2DW77. That's been the subject of a couple of requests. I think we'll be able to work on it a little more to get some detail. 2DW50 is Mr. Tomovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll leave it at there for the time being, and then depending on the outcome of your further consultations, we'll come back to you or you come back to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: One last note, Mr. President, I think to clarify for everybody's sake. If we are looking at the list of witnesses for the month of September that was filed I think on the 14th or 15th of August, the one that lists week five and week six, we discussed this last night as well. There are two witnesses listed who I think have been now withdrawn because one - and this is 2DW58 - was actually admitted pursuant to Rule 92 bis pursuant to the Court's 10 July order. I think we are in agreement that he is not coming. Then there's 2DW61 who my friend withdraw in his 16 July filing, so he is not coming, and that's beside the three other witnesses that were withdrawn in one of my friend's filings: 2DW30, 54, and 53.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So we can start with the new witness. Good morning to you, sir. Did you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning to you, and welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are about to start giving evidence, and before you do so, you are required to enter a solemn declaration that you will be speaking the truth. The text is being handed to you now, please read it out aloud, but please stand up, first of all. Please read out that declaration aloud, and that will be injury solemn undertaking with us. It's equivalent to an oath in some jurisdictions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Nikolic from the Beara Defence team will be putting some questions to you. Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Alaica.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I will introduce myself. My name is Predrag Nikolic, attorney at law, member of the Defence team of Mr. Ljubisa Beara. I will pose questions today on behalf of the Defence team. May we move on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Alaica, I will ask you to introduce yourself so that we will have that on the record.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: My name is Milan Alaica, father's name Dragan, mother's name Mila, born in 1954, in the village of Pescenica [phoen], municipality of Vrgin Most, the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What is your educational background?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: I completed the School of the Interior and additional courses during my career. I did two courses in particular, one for encryption special list and another for a forensic technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What was your employment like, Mr. Alaica?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: I used to work in Split in the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia until the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What were your jobs with the ministry?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: I began as a beat policeman, and then I advanced. After having completed the encryption course, I was moved to the encryption department in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that you worked in Split until the war. Why did you say that? Is that when you stopped working?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: Yes. I stopped working in 1991 when the all-familiar events began taking place in Croatia. For those of us who were Serbs, there was no place in the governmental offices of the Republic of Croatia. I was demoted from my position for a while. I again was returned to be a patrolman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, we need to have a break of about ten to 15 minutes, please. --- Break taken at 9.51 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, during the break, I received a note from the registry that we should ascertain what the precise last name of the witness is. In the transcript, we have "Alaica." It may well be that I misspoke, and perhaps we should clarify that issue, first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Alaica, could you please tell us precisely what your last name is slowly, so that we could have it recorded correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: A-l-a-i-c-a, without a J.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe we can move on. I want to remind you that we left off when you started talking about the problems at work. How did you deal with them? Did you remain with the Ministry of the Interior or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: I did not. There was no possibility to leave Split since the town was blocked. My family was mistreated. Since I knew Mr. Beara, since before the war, say from 1998 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1988.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- when he moved into the apartment next to my brother's apartment. My brother's name is Bosko. Bosko was also a member of the JNA. My brother, Bosko, advised me to talk to Mr. Beara, so that we could see what the possibilities are of me being transferred to the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What year was that and what period, what month, when all this was taking place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: This was taking place between May 1991 and the 1st of November, 1991, when I was officially received by the military police battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What were your duties in the military police battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: My duties were that of a desk clerk in charge of combatting crime and all other tasks that had to do with the department for the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The MP battalion, where was it located at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: The battalion command was in the Dracevac Barracks. It's units were assigned to different facilities, important facilities, and barracks, to provide security. That was in Split and its environs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You said that was in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What was the ethnic makeup of the MP battalion at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: The ethnic makeup was -- well, it was small Yugoslavia, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: There were Muslims, Croats, Serbs from all parts of Yugoslavia, Macedonians, Slovenians, Siptars.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: During that period, could the MP battalion function normally and move about the city?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: No. For the most part, we had big problems because their barracks was blocked as well by the then-paramilitary formations, even if we talk from the point of view of the Croatian government. Those formations were preventing any movement on the part of the military police members as well as all the other JNA units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you recall who was the then-MP battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: It was -- I cannot remember exactly. In any case, his deputy was Bajat Velimir who later became commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At the time, how could the MP battalion commander organise its functioning, as well as the functioning of its different departments?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: With great difficulty. With the assistance of the Superior Command and its security department, that was headed by Mr. Beara who coordinated the work of the battalion vis-a-vis the navy war command, as well as any talks that were to take place with the monitors of the then-European Community. They were in charge of coordination, and, therefore, to a certain extent, they could enable the battalion to function in a certain way under the limited conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Were you able to observe Mr. Beara in action and how he went about his work in order to resolve the problems?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Because when I joined the MP battalion as an experienced policeman, I was assigned precisely to the navy command where Mr. Beara was as well. In other words, I was there on the premises and I took part in some security tasks during the talks and the negotiations and the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me some of his specific actions that reflect -- or rather, tell me, how did he behave towards resolving the situation that the MP battalion found itself in?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: Since at the time the families of the MP battalion were in danger, Mr. Beara spent most of his time in trying to rescue the women and the children of us members of the military police, as well as of other officers from other units. So, in all these talks and negotiations, he tried to obtain permissions for these people since they were actually confined in their residences to be transferred to the barracks in order to reunite with their fathers, husbands, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How did you manage at all to do your daily job with such a great number of civilians arriving at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: We organised ourselves by allocating a number of rooms. We vacated them, removed all the military equipment and the officers who were there, and we housed the women and the children in these rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We are talking about now the MP battalion at the command, but you also said that there were members of the military police outside of the city securing certain facilities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What was the situation with these members of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: The major problem or the biggest problem was the attached facility in Zrnovnica. It was secured by one of our companies commanded by Lieutenant Senad Burzic, and his deputy was Rajko Milovanovic. For the most part, this unit was made up of various -- members of various ethnicities, but they were all professionals so these were professional military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Before I ask you the next question, can you please now repeat the exact name of this facility that you just mentioned, please say it very loudly and clearly so that it can be recorded?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: Zrnovnica, Z-r-n-o-v-n-i-c-a.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You said that the most serious problem was with the security at this location. Why was that and what problems were there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: This facility was of vital importance for the defence of the city of Split and central Adriatic coast, because in it were rocket launchers and other coastal artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Were there any attacks launched on this facility?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: From day one when the conflict started, this facility was besieged and surrounded by paramilitary units of the Republic of Croatia; and every day and every night, it was attacked and fired on from small arms and from mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Were there any casualties among members of the battalion as a result of these attacks?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: Yes, there were. In one of the more serious attacks, the company commander, Senad Burzic, was wounded, as well as his deputy, Rajko Milovanovic, and also a couple of soldiers but I don't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What happened with this man, Burzic, and his deputy? Where were they taken after they had been wounded?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: At first, for the whole day, the paramilitary did not allow any medical assistance to be given to them. Then, on the assistance of Mr. Beara for the European Community, observers to come to the navy command. He wanted to -- an agreement to be reached on how to place these people in hospital. They arrived in the afternoon, talks were held, and, as a result, an ambulance was allowed to come in and evacuate the wounded to hospital. They were taken to a civilian hospital in Split, although there was a military hospital in Split as well, but they were taken to the civilian hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, or rather, do you know what kind of wounds Burzic sustained?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: Senad Burzic sustained serious bodily injuries, his leg was amputated; and Rajko Milovanovic was wounded to the head; and the other soldiers sustained light injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How was this problem with Senad Burzic and his deputy who were wounded was solved? Where did they receive medical help?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: Since the navy command received information - that is to say, Mr. Beara received it - that the wounded were not properly taken care of, he again insisted on the EC observers organising and allowing the wounded to be taken over from the Split hospital, and be transferred to the medical -- military medical academy in Belgrade. That was done after some time. They were airlifted by helicopter to the military medical academy in Belgrade where they received proper medical care.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you know Senad Burzic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any follow-up information about what happened to him after he had been transferred to the military hospital in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: After the unit was relocated from Split to Kumbor in Montenegro, we received information that Senad Burzic was discharged from the military hospital and that he had gone to visit his parents in a village near Sanski Most in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Where was the unit billeted at the time, and what time of period are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: On the 5th of February, the whole unit gathered together in Kumbor in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you maintain contact with these wounded members of the MP battalion, Burzic and the others? What happened to them afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Depending on the possibilities and the available communications, lines, telephones and the like, we maintained permanent contact with our members irrespective of their whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What was the role -- or rather, how did Ljubisa Beara act as the head of the security department after the unit had been relocated? Did he show any interest in these individuals bearing in mind that there was contact where -- between the MP battalion and the security department?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: Yes. He took care of every single member of the battalion; and in May, information was received that Senad Burzic was having problems in his village where he was visiting his parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What problems are we talking about, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: As we understand, there were some combat operations around Sanski Most, and Senad Burzic and his wife and children tried to get out of the area and the combat zone with the help of JNA members -- or rather, a member of the JNA that he had been acquainted with from the time he attended the academy, he was transferred to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We have to break now. I am, after consulting with my colleagues, reducing it to 20 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Alaica, you said that the entire command moved to a new location in Kumbor. What about the MP battalion as well as the other units, did they keep the mixed ethnic makeup that they used to have in Split?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: Yes, they did. The ethnic makeup of the battalion remained the same to that one in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: New location, new work organisation. What was the behaviour of Mr. Beara to the people who were of different ethnicities, other ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: Beara was an exceptional officer in the sense that he respected each and every member regardless of their ethnicity or any other affiliation. It could particularly be seen through the prism of his head of security. It was Lieutenant Nermin Jusic who was a Muslim. In the that department, there were other ethnicities represented as well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Sergeant, rather than Lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat the name of the person you mentioned who was with the security. You said Jusic, but his first name was not recorded?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: The commander of his department or his unit for security and escort was Nermin Jusic, sergeant first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you cite and example of what you called fair behaviour of Mr. Beara vis-a-vis the number of other ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: Let's go back to Senad Burzic that we mentioned. When we learned that he was experiencing problems in Bosnia, where there was combat between some paramilitary Serb and Muslim formations, Beara ordered our commander to dispatch a vehicle to Belgrade, and to transfer Burzic's family from Belgrade to Kumbor so that we could be closer to him and his family and to assist him through the rough times. As regards other ethnicities, all those who wanted to relocate outside Croatia to Bosnia, Serbia, Montenegro, regardless of their ethnicity, it was Ljubisa who helped all of them. He secured transport of both their families and property.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The events related to Senad Burzic, when was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: Sometime in the spring of 1992. I don't remember any exact dates. After he arrived, I think it was sometime in April, his arrival in Kumbor, he told us what he had been through and how he had faired. He also -- he also used his leg prosthesis as he was flying through the woods. Since he could move with difficulty using the crutches and without his prosthesis, during a meeting and upon Beara's proposal, it was decided that we should all contribute one per diem in order to buy him a new prosthesis that was purchased in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Alaica, you said that the commander of a military police unit was Nermin Jusic. I'm interested in your opinion. Did Beara truly believe and trust the people of other ethnicities, or was he just putting up an act to try to keep the semblance of this mixed ethnic makeup?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Objection, speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Alaica, we don't want you to speculate. We want you to tell us, if you can, if you succeeded in forming an opinion on this, based on what you saw, whether you can make an assessment, without speculating. If you don't know, if you have doubts, you just keep your mouth shut then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my opinion concerning Ljubisa's conduct towards the members of other ethnicities is a very positive one. At no moment could one feel him making any difference between any of us members of the battalion belonging to different ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you specify another example to further corroborate your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: In early May 1992, Nermin Jusic complained that his family was in danger in Bratunac. He asked if he could be helped. He went to see Ljubisa. Ljubisa ordered our commander that I should report to his office. When I arrived in his office, he offered me to sit down, to have coffee, much as he did with each and every officer that would come to his office. He lay the problem on the table. He said that an officer of our family is in danger in Bratunac and that it would be good if we could pull them out of that area to a free area. At a certain point, Sergeant Jusic was led into the office as well, and Ljubisa again told me then this: "If you believe that this would put your life in danger, I am not going to order you to do this in military terms, but I would rather ask you, person to person, to help this man and his family." Since I was the most experienced in the battalion and all of the others were junior to me, save for the commander, I said that, yes, I would take that on and that I will do what can be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When was that in what month and year, and where were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: It was in the first half of May 1992. We were in Kumbor in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you respond positively to Mr. Beara's plea, and, of course, to Mr. Jusic's?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me briefly how you went about that? Did you, in fact, manage to reach Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please answer the question. We don't see that it's a leading question. Sorry to the interpreters. We don't see it as a leading question. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We organised ourselves in a fashion that I went there, together with Sergeant Jusic and another soldier driver, with our MP vehicle. It was an off-road vehicle, a jeep. We set out the same day in the afternoon, arriving sometime in the evening around 9 p.m. to Uzice. We rested there, had dinner, refueled, and gathered information on how we should proceed further, in what direction. This, we learned from members of the internal organs in Uzice. In Uzice, we were told that it was not advisable to go in that since there was combat. I insisted that I go regardless of what the nature of combat was. Early the next morning, I set out together with the driver and Jusic, arriving at far as Ljubovija. Once there, on the other side of the Drina from the direction of Bratunac, one could hear firing and explosions. We presumed, therefore, that there was still combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, I want to interrupt you for a second. Where is Ljubovija, in what republic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: The Republic of Serbia, it's across Bratunac, the Drina is between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How did you cross the river to reach Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: Once we arrived in Ljubovija, I reported to the Crisis Staff with the intention of learning what the possibilities were to cross the river and to seek any approvals that I might need to enter Bosnia; however, they refused to issue any sort of pass. They just told me that I was going there at my own risk, that is there was combat, and that they advised me not to go. In the meantime, while I was negotiating with the people from the Crisis Staff, Nermin Jusic recognised some of the people in front of the building in the street. One of those people told him that his mother, brother, and sister were in Ljubovija accommodated with a family friend of their father's, Jusic's father, and that we should go and look for them there. When I came out of the building, Jusic told me that we should go to a house nearby since his brother, sister, and mother were supposed to be there. Once we got to the house, we found, indeed, his mother, brother, and sister there. His mother began to cry. She kneeled down and started kissing my boots. I wouldn't have that, I asked her to get up on my feet. I told her that I was doing that as a duty of mine and that I did that following the where of Mr. Ljubisa Beara and her son Nermin who initiated the whole operation. In our further discussion with the mother, she told us that in Bratunac, there was still Nermin's grandmother there on his father's side, and that they had no information on her. They, however, arrived in Ljubovija without any footwear or clothes, without any IDs and money. I decided that we should go to Bratunac regardless of the circumstances. Nermin's mother asked me to try and find some personal documents, if we can, and also to bring back some clothes. She asked me to go into a small cellar under the stairs in the house, telling me that there was a plastic bag under a barrel there containing some of their valuables like gold, some money, things that any house would have, family jewellery. And she asked me to bring that back in case I found it. After awhile, we set out; I mean, myself, Nermin and the driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And did you reach the house?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: When we arrived at the bridge on the Drina, the police of the Republic of Serbia was securing the Serbian side, and they told us that they couldn't let us pass through because there was fighting going on there. I explained to them briefly that I was on a mission, that it was not their problem, that it was my problem, that they should let me go through, and that is what they did. When we crossed over to the other side and entered the municipality of Bratunac, we were met on the bridge by some armed civilians who had no proper uniforms or insignia. They were armed with some outdated weapons from the second World War. They were looking very untidy. They behaved arrogantly, started to threaten us, and told us that they would not let us go to Bratunac. After some serious argument and quarrel with them, we were persistent and we somehow managed to make them let us go through and arrived in Bratunac. When we reached the centre of the town, Nermin told me on the way that it would be best if we dropped by at the municipal building because that is where the Crisis Staff was headquartered and to ask them for help, so that we can move more freely around Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can I just interrupt you for a second. At the time, were you wearing the military police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: Yes. We had proper uniforms. We had small arms. Our vehicle was marked as a proper military police vehicle with all the stickers and rotation lights and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So dressed in your uniforms and driving such a vehicle, you crossed over to the Bratunac where you were accosted by these paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: When we arrived in front of the municipal building, there was a number of people dressed in various clothes. We could hear shots coming from the direction of the hotel. Everyone was nervous and anxious. They walked towards us and tried to disarm us and to confiscate our vehicle. I confronted them and said that I was on a mission and that I was on my way to see the president of the Crisis Staff. We somehow managed to enter the building, the municipal building. In the hall of the building, there was a civilian with a beard, armed with a machine gun from the second World War. He stopped us and said that we couldn't enter the building and see the president. We started quarrelling with him there. At one point, a civilian emerged from one of the offices, I remember that he had a leather cap on his head, and he asked what was all this about, why we were arguing. Nermin then addressed him and said -- and called him "Professor." This man turned towards Nermin and said, "Nermin, is that you?" And he said, "Yes, it is me." They embraced each other, and we explained to him why we came. After that, he took us to the office of the president of the Crisis Staff. When we entered the office, the president of the Crisis Staff was very abrasive. He was in a hurry. He was constantly answering the phone or the radio and receiving information and/or exchanging information because there was allegedly fighting going on in the vicinity of the motel, and in the village, as I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Alaica, did you manage to reach Nrmin's house?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: When we explained to him that our intention was to go to the house in order to pick up his family's documents and valuables and to see what was happening with his grandmother, he said that he had no objection to that, but that he thought it would be ill-advised for us to go there because there was fighting in the town. We told him that we were determined to go regardless of any fighting and asked him to give us one man, if possible, to accompany us for the purpose of security and for moving around the town better. This professor then offered to accompany us himself. We all got into the car and went to his house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, we have been extremely, extremely patient, but it has come to a stage where we have to bring it to order. None of this appeared in the summaries. You are going into much detail that has absolutely no relevance. Please stick to the reason why you summoned this witness. All this is unnecessary, completely irrelevant. I don't know why you are wasting your and our time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, Your Honour. I was just about to ask the witness to finish this story. And if you allow me to continue, I shall finish shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bosko -- excuse me, Mr. Milan [sic], your intention was to locate the family and you reached the house. Did you find Mr. Jusic's grandmother; and, tell us briefly, did you succeed in your intentions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: Yes. We found the documents and everything else that his mother had asked for, then we went to his grandmother's house which was in the centre of the town. Once there, Nermin alighted from the car and entered the house, but he didn't find his grandmother there. He came out again where the professor and I were standing in the street, and at that moment the shooting quietened. A woman came out of the neighbouring house across the street, and she asked us who we were looking for. Nermin recognised her and told her that we were looking for his grandmother. She told him that she was in the cellar of her house. Nermin went with her to her house, took out his grandmother, we put her in into the car and headed for Ljubovija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you manage to get back to Ljubovija?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: As soon as we reached the bridge on the Drina, we again encountered the same problems with the same men that we had had on our way there, but there were many more of them now. I also noticed that we had been followed by a car --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Alaica, I have to interrupt you here. You set off on this trip in order to save the family of Mr. Jusic. Did you manage to reunite the family, and did you manage to rescue them from this environment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We gathered them all together and took them to Kumbor in Montenegro where they stayed until their departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you report about all this to Ljubisa Beara?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And tell us at the end what his reaction was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ALAICA
utterances.text: He was very pleased with how we accomplished the mission, and he was very happy to see the family united in one place and that they were able to help each other in their further life.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Alaica. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, you had asked for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will not cross-examine this witness, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Ms. Nikolic, just for a quarter of an hour?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I have no questions. Thank you, madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, you had asked for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau, you asked for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no other question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. Mr. Krgovic, no cross-examination, confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Sarapa, you had asked for 15 minutes, but you require none.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't have any further questions for you, which means that your testimony comes to an end here. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I thank you for having come over to give testimony; and on behalf of everyone present, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that disposes of this witness. We can bring in the next one. It is Mrs. Cekic, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President. Just two minor items with respect to this witness. At the last break, I had an opportunity to speak with her briefly, and there's a typographical error on the 65 ter summary, and I advised my learned friend of that. It's 1985. I believe that we'll hear that evidence, but I know Mr. Thayer is asking. So I wasn't sure if he got that message. I did speak to Mr. McCloskey in connection with that. The other issue, Mr. President, involves a personal matter with respect to this witness and I'd like just to share it with the Court, because during her testimony, I'd like to go into private session because it's a sensitive issue, but I'd like to advise you about it prior to me doing so, so that you can either permit me or I'm deny me the right to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I can go into private session now, so I can explain it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are most welcome to this Tribunal and in this case, where you are going to give evidence as a Defence witness for accused Beara. Before you start giving your testimony, our Rules require that you make a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony YOU will be speaking the truth. Madam Usher, the lady who is standing next to you, is going to hand you the text of the declaration. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, madam, please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we go into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ostojic. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. There is something wrong at page 39, line 7, yes, about the last name of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think, if I can, just for the record, Mr. President, just have her name -- it's Miroslava, M-i-r-o-s-l-a-v-a. Then on line 7 of page 39, I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The word "Zivanovic" has to disappear. We don't want to complicate your private life, Mr. Zivanovic. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Cekic. As you know, my name is John Ostojic. I'm one of the attorneys for Mr. Ljubisa Beara, and we are going to ask you a few questions here today. I'm going to ask you and try not to speak quickly so that you can fully understand the question, and I'll give you an opportunity to answer the question. Initially, for the record, can you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: Miroslava Cekic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Kindly share with us your date of birth, and not necessarily the year, but you can do so if you desire, and your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: 16th of May, 1949. The place of birth is Curug.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: For those of us who may not be the place of Curug, can you tell us in what country that is?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: That's Serbia, and the nearest big town is Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Madam Cekic, I would like to ask a little bit about your background. Can you tell us the extent of your education and what is the highest level of education that you've attained?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: I finished the PTT secondary school in the late 1974; and in the same year, I found employment at the PTT Yugoslavia, as it was called then. And I'm still employed; only now it is called Telecom Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just describe briefly for us the job duties or the capacity of your employment with PTT Serbia, or Telecom Serbia, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: I used to work in the maintenance department until three and a half years ago; and since these PTT devices are obsolete, they have been replaced by newer ones. And I was transferred to the trade union organisation of Telecom Serbia, and this is where I'm still working.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, may we please go into private session for the next couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us what your late husband did for purposes of employment, to get an understanding of his background?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: My late husband worked for Split-Jadro company, a flower distribution company. A shipment of flowers arrived every day from Split to Belgrade, and he would distribute it to the flower dealers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Nada Beara?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Nada Beara was my late husband's supervisor, and she also worked for Split Jadro in Split. And they communicated along this business lines and relations, but later on it turned into a friendship and they used to get together whenever Nada would come to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to meet and know Mr. Ljubisa Beara?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I later met Mr. Ljubisa Beara as well, whenever he had an opportunity to accompany Nada to Belgrade when she attended flower exhibitions or when there was a meeting that she had to have with your business associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so I can have the time parameters, when did this business relationship or working relationship between Ms. Nada Beara and your late husband, Tomo, begin?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: Well, it all began in 1985. That is when I met Mrs. Nada Beara. They had probably known each other before. I don't remember exactly when this flower business was started and when these shipments started arriving from Split to Belgrade. But in the years after 1985, we used to meet occasionally when she was on business in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And share with us, if you will, when the social relationship with you and your late husband and the Bearas began?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: Well, we started socialising in 1991 when Nada and her younger son, Branco, came to Belgrade from Split, and that is where they continued living.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Give us the general idea how often from 1991 would you socialize with the Bearas?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: Well, whenever we had time, we would speak on the phone during the week. Sometimes during the weekends on Friday evenings or Saturday evenings, we would get together either at their place or at our place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And thank you for that. I think I understand. But give me an idea: Was it once a month, once a week, every several months, or rarely, often? You mentioned the dates on the Saturdays and Fridays, but I still don't have an appreciation, with all due respect, how often and how regular you would meet with the Bearas.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: We would see each other depending on the amount of time we had when we would be free of obligations. This includes both my late husband and myself. However, we would speak on the phone at least once or twice within any given week.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember during the period of -- and are you still maintaining a social relationship with Nada Beara at least?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I know you haven't seen Mr. Ljubisa Beara for a few years, but did you maintain -- or share with us whether or not you maintained a social relationship with both Nada and Ljubisa Beara up to and including the year 2004?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we socialized. We saw each other in 2000. That is when my husband died and they attending the funeral; Nada and Ljubisa, that is. Before that, we would see each other as friends, visiting their home, or they visited us for coffee or a meal. In 2001, on the first anniversary of my husband's death, Mr. Ljubisa attended the memorial church service with me, and Nada was unable to attend at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to change a little bit. Are you familiar with the name of an individual by Milan Stanic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Tell us, to the best of your knowledge, who he is?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: Milan Stanic is an attorney at law. I believe he is a member of the Beara Defence team. I met him this year in late February when he returned from the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that detail in a little bit. Thank you for that. Prior to February of 2008, did you know or ever meet Milan Stanic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, just so the record so we have a complete record, when was the first time that you met me, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: I saw you for the first time this summer, I believe, in mid-August.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And with me, is that the first time that you met Mr. Peter Nikolic, who is also counsel for Mr. Beara, to my left?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to Milan Stanic, and you were starting to tell us about the circumstances upon your first meeting with him in February of 2008. Can you tell us where that meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: I was visiting Nada; and after awhile, Mr. Stanic arrived as well. That is how we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I am sorry to interrupt you. I just want to be as specific as possible on some of these details. You were visiting Nada where?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: In her house.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Then please proceed. I am sorry. Then you started to tell us that Mr. Stanic arrived at the house or at the apartment of the Bearas, and then was there anyone else present at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: No. It was just Nada, myself, and Mr. Stanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you engage in any conversation at that time in February of 2008 with Mr. Stanic at the Beara apartment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since he said he had visited Ljubisa, I asked him how he was doing, what he looked like, and whether he was all right. He told me that he looked well, that he was doing well; then we started talking about this and that, about what was happening and was still happening in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Approximately how long did you have this meeting with Mr. Stanic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: I sat there for about an hour and a half, maybe two.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you discuss at any time inclusive of the February 2008 period with Mr. Stanic the potential for you to be a prospective witness on behalf of Ljubisa Beara?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: He asked me how long I knew Ljubisa. He asked me what sort of a person he was and whether we were friends, and I responded to most of his questions positively. He asked me whether we used to see each other when Ljubisa came, and since I knew that Ljubisa was in the Republika Srpska, whether we saw each other at that time. I told him that, indeed, we saw him, that he would call by phone, and we socialised time permitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you share with Mr. Stanic any other details, and particularly things that may have occurred in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stanic asked me if I remembered any details or meetings during 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And how did you respond?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: I told him that there were things I remembered. It was quite a long time ago when you count the years, but there are details that one remembers and does not forget easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would you mind sharing it with us? What are some of those details with respect to 1995 that you told Mr. Stanic? What is it that you remember?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAVA CEKIC
utterances.text: I remember, for instance, that in 1995 by that time our financial situation was not so good. We all know that as early as 1991 or 1992, there were no more flower shipments coming to Belgrade from Split. The company focused itself on a different flower operation. It was by that time called Beo-Jadro. My husband was still working for them, and they were getting flowers from the countries surrounding Serbia. I could recall certain meetings; and as long as the money lasted, we were able to go on holidays, my husband and I. But by 1994 and 1995, the money had run out. We had difficulties making our ends meet. Since in May there's my birthday - on that day, Ljubisa was in Belgrade - I invited both him and Nada to come over, not for the sake of the birthday, but simply to sit down together and chat. Since he was a merry person, he was attentive and he liked bringing small presents.
